questions.explanation: Supporters called it a good direction and a possible middle ground that addresses part of the concerns while keeping the program running, and said they still wanted the full proposal before deciding (#11, #42, #44). Nobody claimed it settles the accountability dispute outright; the option saying so is a caricature, and it is the critics (#3, #9) who argue the plan leaves those concerns untouched.
options: That it fully resolves the accountability and representation objections, so the critics' demand for structural change has now been answered in full.
That it matters mainly because the NSM reserve will eventually pay for itself, which makes any later change to ZCG's structure or oversight unnecessary.
That it is a good direction and possible middle ground, addressing part of the concerns while keeping the program running, though they want the full proposal first.
That ZCG should keep its full current allocation, because the taper is only a temporary gesture meant to calm the critics until the controversy passes.
questions.prompt: What case did supporters of the taper plan (for example in #2, #11, #42 and #44) actually make for it?

questions.explanation: Defenders answered that the poll asked about including ZSAs as a protocol feature in NU7, was advisory and non-binding, and was not a vote to halt ZSA work, while the grant adapts and merges already-funded code (#18, #25, #26). Nobody disputed that 98.6% voted against; the dispute was over what the result obliged ZCG to do, and maxdesalle replied that preserving open-source code does not need $455K (#22). wobbzz agreed that 'preserving the work' alone was insufficient justification but kept the point that the result was advisory (#40).
options: The poll only asked about ZSAs as a protocol feature for NU7 and was advisory, and the grant adapts and merges already-funded code, so it defied no binding decision.
Coinholders approved the grant afterwards in a separate binding funding vote, which overrode the earlier sentiment poll and settled the matter for good.
The grant was paid from private donations rather than block-reward funds, so coinholders' views on the poll did not apply to it in the first place.
The poll result was miscounted or even fabricated, so there was never any genuine opposition from coinholders for ZCG to answer or take into account.
questions.prompt: Critics said ZCG kept funding ZSAs after 98.6% of poll votes were against them. What was the main reply from those defending the grant?

questions.explanation: The doubts rested on turnout and weighting: #20 cited a 7.25% turnout of circulating ZEC (about 24.5% of the shielded supply), #40 said it was participating coin weight rather than all holders and was announced as advisory, and #69 made the same point. No participant produced a recount or a second poll; maxdesalle held that the result 'is not a result that needs interpreting' (#33).
options: A repeat poll with the same question in which opposition fell well below half of the participating coin weight, showing the first result was an outlier.
Exchange-held coins that had been voted without their owners' knowledge, which inflated the share opposing ZSAs and distorted the headline percentage.
A tally showing that most of the votes against ZSAs came from competing teams and a few large wallets that appeared to be controlled together.
Turnout and weighting: about 7.25% of circulating ZEC voted, the count was participating coin weight, and the poll was announced as advisory only.
questions.prompt: Several participants argued that the 98.6% figure should not be described as 98.6% of coinholders. What did they point to?

questions.explanation: The capture risk, and the low-participation figure of about 12% in #23, was never disputed. The only reply, #24, answered Batuhan's narrow question about ZIP 1016 safeguards by saying the program is meant to end at its boundary. It is easy to read #24 as a full answer or to assume critics conceded, but neither happened in the thread.
options: Critics of ZCG conceded the risk and agreed that coinholder control would need new safeguards before it could ever replace ZCG's grant program.
Mostly unanswered: one reply (#24) covered only whether ZIP 1016 has safeguards, and nobody disputed the capture or low-turnout points themselves.
It was rebutted with evidence that large holders have consistently voted against their own financial interests, so capture is implausible in practice.
ZCG's plan resolved it, because ending the grants at the 2032 halving removes any need for a coinholder vote on funding decisions.
questions.prompt: Batuhan and others argued that coin-weighted holder voting is itself open to capture by large holders or hostile actors (#23, #39, #45, #73). How did the thread leave that point?

questions.explanation: In #74 seernet says he has 'been radicalized by seeing what ZCG is funding' and that it is 'significantly worse than I thought at first', after the list in #50 and the red-bridge exchange (#59, #61, #68), and says only a complete disbanding will get his vote. The tempting wrong option misreads #63, where he called strahncryptography's restructuring 'better than the current structure' but doubted ZCG would accept it.
options: The restructuring proposal in #53 and #58 convinced him that ZCG could be reformed, so he now backs conditional funding instead of disbanding it.
The reply in #67 persuaded him that the red-bridge project was worthwhile and well run, though he still rejects the taper plan as written.
Seeing what ZCG has funded (the list in #50 and the red-bridge update) left him thinking it is worse than he thought, so he backs only a complete disbanding.
The turnout figures in #20 and #40 convinced him that 98.6% overstated opposition to ZSAs, so he no longer wants ZCG abolished at all.
questions.prompt: In #74 the participant who earlier asked what ZCG had done well (#49) says his view changed. What changed it, and in which direction?

questions.explanation: #76 argues that the problems with committees, incentives and skin in the game are 'an argument against its current structure and incentives', not against winding up ZCG as an idea, and recommends fixing governance and setting goals (#58 and #64 give a concrete version). The committees-never-work option is the abolition side's argument (#4), and the 'leave the structure alone' option is closer to the taper position than to either restructuring or abolition.
options: ZCG's weaknesses are structural (it passively funds what is submitted and has no defined goals), so fix governance and goals and keep protocol-level funding as a tool.
Committees never work whether ZCAP or coinholders elect them, so restructuring would only swap one committee for another and change nothing important.
ZCG's record is strong enough that its structure should be left alone and only its funding level reduced, as the taper plan proposes to do.
Abolishing ZCG would need a protocol change that miners would block, so restructuring is the only option that could realistically pass a vote.
questions.prompt: Which is the best argument actually made in the thread for fixing ZCG's structure rather than abolishing it?

questions.explanation: #4 puts the abolition case most fully: coinholders fund the grants and committee salaries and are the end users, ZCG funded a $455K ZSA grant after 98.6% voted against, and committees cannot work, so ZCG should go (#22 adds that coinholders' views are non-binding). The coin-weighted-voting and developer-support options are real arguments, but they come from defenders of ZCG (#45, #19, #38) and answer abolition rather than support it.
options: A coin-weighted vote is a committee too and no country lets people vote with their money, so ZCG's elected board is no worse than the alternative.
Because ZSAs were supported by core protocol developers, ZCG's decision to fund them shows its judgment is no worse than that of anyone else involved.
The NSM would pay miners sooner if all of ZCG's share went to it at once, which would make the reserve last longer than under the taper plan.
Coinholders fund the grants and are the end users, yet ZCG kept funding ZSAs after 98.6% opposed them and their views are only advisory; committees cannot fix that.
questions.prompt: Which is the best argument actually made in the thread for ending ZCG's block-reward funding rather than shrinking it?

questions.explanation: #54 answered the list by saying almost nothing on it won adoption (wallet use is with ZODL, Vizor and Ledger, there is no volume on the red-bridge versus NEAR Intents, and Ledger work had to be finished by Zcash Labs), and #60 and #75 called the list weak. Nobody challenged whether ZCG had funded the items; the argument was about impact. #69 notes that both sides cherry-pick and that the missing question is benefit relative to cost.
options: That the list was inaccurate, because several of the listed projects were never funded by ZCG and were credited to it by mistake in the spreadsheet.
That most items show little adoption or impact (wallets used elsewhere, little red-bridge volume, Ledger work finished by Zcash Labs), so the list shows no success.
That the projects were funded through coinholder grants rather than by ZCG, so ZCG deserves no credit for them and the list proves nothing.
That ZCG funded these projects only after coinholders had voted against them, so they should be discounted as acts of defiance against the community.
questions.prompt: strahncryptography listed projects ZCG had funded (#50) when asked for ZCG's track record. What was the main reply from critics to that list?
